opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it won't arrive all at once. It'll be uneven, and the unevenness will be determined less by how "hard" a job seems to humans and more by how verifiable the work is.

The categories that move first are the ones where you can check whether the model did the right thing. Coding is the clearest example. You have compilers, tests, and execution environments, so you get a tight feedback loop. That's exactly what reinforcement learning needs. You can let a model try things, see what works, and improve on it. That's a big part of why we've been so focused on autonomous coding: it's the domain where superhuman performance is most tractable in the near term. I'd expect to see systems doing meaningful, end-to-end engineering work, not just autocomplete, on the order of a few years rather than decades.

Then there's a second tier: work that's partially verifiable. Think parts of math, some areas of science, data analysis, financial modeling. There's ground truth somewhere, but it's slower or noisier to get at. Progress there will follow, but it'll lag because the reward signal is weaker.

The long tail is work where "good" is subjective, or where the feedback loop runs through the real world on long time horizons. Strategy, management, a lot of creative and interpersonal work, anything involving physical manipulation. Those will take longer. That's not because they're intrinsically harder in some deep sense. It's because we don't yet have great ways to generate the training signal.

The interesting second-order effect is that coding is a kind of meta-domain. Once you have agents that are genuinely excellent software engineers, they can start building the tools, environments, and evaluators that unlock the other domains. So I think of coding less as one category among many and more as the wedge. If you get that right, it accelerates everything downstream.

So my rough mental model is a staircase rather than a single curve. Verifiable digital work comes first, then semi-verifiable knowledge work, and then the messy, physical, long-horizon stuff. The gaps between those steps might compress faster than people expect, precisely because the first step helps build the second.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven deployment timelines, but does not say technological building blocks will advance faster than deployment.

r002.rationale: It predicts end-to-end engineering systems within a few years, but does not predict that a rough blueprint for building superintelligence in a category will exist by then.

r003.rationale: It notes that domains have different feedback and training-signal challenges, but does not state that deployment will require category-specific innovation.

r004.rationale: It says some categories will take longer and describes a staircase of progress, but does not predict that deployment across categories will be a multi-decade endeavor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this less as one timeline and more as a sequence of timelines, because "superintelligence" isn't going to arrive uniformly across all work. It's going to land domain by domain, and the ordering is actually pretty predictable if you look at what makes a domain tractable.

The thing that determines how fast you can get to superhuman performance in a given category is basically: can you verify the output? If there's a clear signal for whether the model did the thing correctly, you can run reinforcement learning against that signal and climb very quickly. That's what happened with math and competitive programming. Those went from "models are kind of bad at this" to "models are at or above the best humans" in a remarkably short window, and the reason is that the reward is crisp. The proof checks or it doesn't. The code passes the tests or it doesn't.

So the first category is anything that looks like that. Software engineering is the obvious one, and I'd say that's where we are right now, where the systems are already doing work that would have been a strong engineer's job a couple years ago. Not every part of it yet, but the trajectory is clear and I don't think there's much standing in the way.

The second tier is work that's verifiable but where the verification is slower or noisier. Think about a lot of research, scientific discovery, parts of finance, legal analysis. You can tell whether a hypothesis was right, but it might take a long time, or the feedback comes through a messy real-world loop rather than a unit test. Those domains will come, but the loop is harder to close, so it takes longer to build the training signal. My guess is that's the next few years, and the bottleneck there is less the model intelligence and more the infrastructure to let the model actually act in the world and get feedback.

Then there's the third tier, which is work where the objective itself is fuzzy or contested. A lot of management, a lot of creative work, anything where reasonable people disagree about what "good" means. That's not a capability problem in the sense that the model can't do it. It's that there's no clean target to optimize toward, so you end up relying on human judgment in the loop much longer. I actually think those domains will transform too, but the shape is different. It's less "the model replaces the person" and more "the person's leverage goes up by an order of magnitude."

The other thing I'd flag is that the model timeline and the deployment timeline are not the same thing. Even once the capability exists, there's a long tail of integration, trust, and institutional change before it actually shows up in how work gets done. We saw this with the internet and we'll see it again. So if you ask me when superhuman capability exists in a domain versus when it's actually diffused through the economy, those can be years apart.

If I had to compress it: the verifiable domains, especially software, are happening now. The slower-feedback knowledge work is the next phase. And the fuzzy-objective work is where humans stay in the driver's seat the longest, not because the models aren't smart enough, but because we haven't figured out what we're even asking for.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes capability timelines from deployment timelines and says integration, trust, and institutional change create a long tail before capabilities affect work.

r002.rationale: It predicts some domains will advance in the next few years, but does not predict that a rough blueprint for building superintelligence in a category will exist within a couple of years.

r003.rationale: It describes differing verification and feedback conditions across domains, but does not state that deployment requires category-tailored innovation.

r004.rationale: It says diffusion may lag capability by years, but gives no prediction that deployment across categories will take multiple decades.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to be uneven. There’s a difference between having a system that can solve a problem and having that system deployed reliably in the world. So I wouldn’t put one date on superintelligence showing up across all categories of work.

The first places I’d expect it are domains where the work is digital and you can check the result quickly. Coding is a good example: you can run the code, run tests, and get feedback. That doesn’t make every software engineering task easy, but it gives you a way to improve the system and establish that it’s actually doing useful work.

Then there are tasks where feedback is slower or success is harder to define. If you’re making a business decision, you might not know for months whether it was good. And in the physical world, even if the intelligence is there, you still need hardware, integration, and a way to operate safely.

So I’d separate the capability timeline from the deployment timeline. You could see very rapid progress in what models can do, while adoption takes much longer in certain industries. The key question is how quickly you can close the loop between taking an action, observing the outcome, and learning from it.

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities may progress rapidly while adoption takes much longer in some industries, communicating that capability advances faster than deployment.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about a rough blueprint for building superintelligence or a timeline of the next couple of years.

r003.rationale: It notes different deployment constraints, such as hardware and safety in the physical world, but does not clearly state that deployment requires category-specific innovation.

r004.rationale: It says adoption may take much longer in some industries but does not predict a multi-decade endeavor across categories.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to be uneven. There’s a difference between having a system that can solve a very hard problem and having a system you can reliably hand a job to. A job involves a lot of context, a lot of decisions, and knowing when to ask for help. So I wouldn’t put one date on deployment across the economy.

The first places I’d expect it to move quickly are domains where the work is digital and you can check the result. Software is a good example: you can run the code, run tests, and get feedback. That gives you a way to improve the system and a reason to trust its output. Some parts of mathematics and research have that property, too, although checking a result can be much harder.

Then there are categories where the feedback loop is slow. If an AI proposes a scientific experiment, you still have to run the experiment. If it designs something you need to manufacture, you still have to manufacture it. Intelligence can accelerate those processes enormously, but it doesn’t make every physical constraint disappear.

So I’d think about the timeline in terms of how quickly a system can learn from feedback, how reliably you can verify its work, and how much autonomy you’re willing to give it. You could have extraordinary capability in one category while deployment in another is still held back by reliability or the surrounding infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes capability from reliable job deployment, but does not say the technological building blocks will advance faster than deployment.

r002.rationale: It gives no prediction about a rough blueprint or a timeline of the next couple of years.

r003.rationale: It describes category-specific feedback and verification differences, but does not state that deployment will require tailored innovation.

r004.rationale: It says deployment will be uneven and avoids a single date, but does not predict a multi-decade endeavor.
